entries.lesson_title: Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs
entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret a complex exponential $e^{j\omega t}$ as a single-frequency probe input for an LTI system, identifying $\omega$ as the frequency whose response determines output scaling and phase.

sections.lesson_title: Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs
sections.section_title: Introduction to Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs

blocks.text: When you analyze an LTI system one frequency at a time, start with the complex exponential input $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$.
Here, $\omega$ is the angular frequency being probed. It is the frequency parameter in the exponent, not the time variable.
Euler's formula shows that this probe is a compact single-frequency representation, not a mixture of frequencies.
Later steps will reuse this same input to read how the LTI system changes the signal's scaling and phase at the same $\omega$.

sections.lesson_title: Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs
sections.section_title: Identifying the Angular Frequency in $e^{j\omega t}$

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=e^{j7t}$, identify the angular frequency and separate it from the imaginary unit and the time variable.

explanation_blocks.text: Compare the signal to the standard probe form $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$.
The coefficient multiplying $t$ inside the exponent is the angular frequency, so here $\omega=7$.
The $j$ is the imaginary unit and $t$ is the time variable; neither one is the frequency parameter.

sections.lesson_title: Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs
sections.section_title: Interpreting $e^{j\omega t}$ as a Single-Frequency Input

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$, decide whether the input is single-frequency or multi-frequency and say what makes it a probe signal.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the standard probe form $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$. This signal is already written with one angular frequency parameter, $\omega$.
Because there is only one exponential frequency present, this is a single-frequency complex exponential, not a mixture of frequencies.
That is why it works as a probe input for an LTI system: it isolates one angular frequency at a time.

sections.lesson_title: Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs
sections.section_title: Using a Complex Exponential to Probe an LTI System

example_content.example_prompt: If you want to probe an LTI system at angular frequency $\omega_0$, what input should you apply and why is that choice useful?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the target frequency $\omega_0$. Use the matching complex exponential input $x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t}$.
This choice is useful because it contains one angular frequency only, so it tests the system one frequency at a time.
The result is a clean probe input: the response at $\omega_0$ can be examined directly next, without mixing in any other frequencies.

sections.lesson_title: Complex Exponentials as LTI System Inputs
sections.section_title: Connecting Probe Frequency to Output Scaling and Phase

example_content.example_prompt: Given a probe input $e^{j\omega_0 t}$, identify which frequency-dependent system response determines the output's scaling and phase.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the probe frequency $\omega_0$. The quantity you want is the system response evaluated at that same frequency, written as the frequency response $H(j\omega_0)$.
The magnitude $|H(j\omega_0)|$ sets the output scaling, and the angle $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ sets the phase shift.
So the probe frequency tells you where to look, and $H(j\omega_0)$ tells you how the system changes that tone without changing the frequency.

entries.lesson_title: Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input
entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the LTI output for $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$ by substituting the input into the convolution integral and factoring out $e^{j\omega t}$ to identify the remaining integral as the system's complex gain at $\omega$.

sections.lesson_title: Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input
sections.section_title: Introduction to Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input

blocks.text: Treat $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$ as a probe input for an LTI system. The goal of this step is to set up the convolution so the factor that depends only on $t$ will be easy to see in the next algebraic move.
Write the convolution in shifted-input form so the substitution matches $x(t-\tau)$ exactly. With that form in place, insert the input as $x(t-\tau)=e^{j\omega(t-\tau)}$.

Now the output is written with the complex exponential inside the integral, and the integrand is ready to be separated into its $t$-dependent and $\tau$-dependent parts. That separation is the move that will expose the system's complex gain at $\omega$.
Keep this setup in mind: the next step will rewrite the exponential, factor out $e^{j\omega t}$, and leave the remaining $\tau$-integral as the frequency-response factor.

sections.lesson_title: Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input
sections.section_title: Substituting $e^{j\omega t}$ into the LTI Convolution Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Start from $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t-\tau)h(\tau)\,d\tau$ and substitute $x(t-\tau)=e^{j\omega(t-\tau)}$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the shifted-input convolution form. The cue is the slot $x(t-\tau)$ inside $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t-\tau)h(\tau)\,d\tau$; in this step, replace only that input term and leave $h(\tau)$ unchanged.
Now substitute the probe input directly into the shifted slot: $x(t-\tau)=e^{j\omega(t-\tau)}$. Keep the $t-\tau$ dependence intact.
That is the finished example result. Stop before factoring out $e^{j\omega t}$; this step is only about making the substitution cleanly.

sections.lesson_title: Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input
sections.section_title: Rewriting $e^{j\omega(t-\tau)}$ to Separate $t$ and $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $e^{j\omega(t-\tau)}$ so the factor depending only on $t$ is separated from the factor depending only on $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted exponential inside the integral. Use the exponent rule to split the factor that depends only on $t$ from the factor that depends only on $\tau$.
Apply the difference rule for exponents: $e^{a-b}=e^ae^{-b}$. Here that gives $e^{j\omega(t-\tau)}=e^{j\omega t}e^{-j\omega\tau}$.
The result is the same integral with the $t$ dependence now isolated as $e^{j\omega t}$. Do not factor it out yet; this step only makes the separation visible.

sections.lesson_title: Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input
sections.section_title: Factoring $e^{j\omega t}$ Outside the Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Take the separated form of the integrand and pull $e^{j\omega t}$ outside the integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $e^{j\omega t}$ does not depend on $\tau$. When a factor is independent of the integration variable, move it outside and leave the $\tau$-integral unchanged.
Now factor out the $t$-only term and keep the remaining $\tau$-dependent part inside the integral.
This is the factored form the later step will interpret. The output now has a pure $t$ factor multiplying a single constant integral.

sections.lesson_title: Deriving the Output for a Complex Exponential Input
sections.section_title: Identifying the Remaining Integral as the Complex Gain at $\omega$

example_content.example_prompt: Recognize the remaining $\tau$-integral as the system's complex gain at $\omega$ and rewrite the output in gain-times-input form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the remaining $\tau$-integral after the factorization step. Name that integral $H(j\omega)$; it is the system's complex gain at the probe frequency.
Define the remaining integral as $H(j\omega)$ so the frequency-dependent system response has a clear name.

Substituting that definition gives the final gain-times-input form. The same complex exponential stays at frequency $\omega$, while the system contributes the complex multiplier $H(j\omega)$, which changes amplitude and phase.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret $H(j\omega)$ as the frequency-indexed complex gain that an LTI system applies to a complex exponential input $e^{j\omega t}$, producing a same-frequency output.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Introduction to Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$

blocks.text: Frequency response is the system's response profile indexed by angular frequency. For each $\omega$, $H(j\omega)$ names the complex gain an LTI system applies at that frequency.
Use $x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t}$ as the probe input. Here $\omega_0$ is the frequency being tested, so the notation asks only how the system responds at that one angular frequency.
Read $H(j\omega_0)$ as the complex gain at angular frequency $\omega_0$. The output keeps the same exponential $e^{j\omega_0 t}$; only the multiplier changes with $\omega$.

blocks.latex: H(j\omega_0)=\text{the complex gain at angular frequency }\omega_0

blocks.text: That is the meaning of frequency response: same frequency in, same frequency out, with the LTI system contributing a frequency-dependent complex multiplier.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Matching a Complex Exponential Input to $H(j\omega_0)$

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system is driven by $x(t)=e^{j6t}$. Identify the frequency-response sample used for this input and write the output in indexed-gain form.

explanation_blocks.text: The exponent tells us the probe frequency is $\omega_0=6$. So the matching frequency-response sample is $H(j6)$, not a generic $H(j\omega)$.
For this probe input, the output stays at the same angular frequency and picks up the complex gain at that frequency.
So the output is the same exponential scaled by $H(j6)$. The only index we had to read from the input was the $6$ inside the exponent.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Interpreting $H(j\omega_0)$ as a Complex Gain

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose an LTI system has $H(j2)=3e^{-j\pi/6}$. Interpret what this value means for the response to $e^{j2t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the index $2$: use the sample $H(j2)$, not a different frequency. Read that sample as the complex multiplier at angular frequency $2$.
So the response to the matching input $e^{j2t}$ is the same input scaled by that gain.
The output stays at frequency $2$. The only change is the complex gain factor.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Writing the Same-Frequency Output Using $H(j\omega_0)$

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{j3t}$ and $H(j3)=1-j$, write the output expression using the same input frequency.

explanation_blocks.text: Match the input frequency to the response sample: the probe is $e^{j3t}$, so the indexed gain is $H(j3)$. Use that gain as a multiplier, not as a new signal.
Write the output by multiplying the input by the indexed gain and keep the exponent unchanged.
The frequency stays at $3$; only the complex factor changes, so the gain belongs in front of the same exponential.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Comparing Complex Gains at Different Frequencies

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system has $H(j1)=2$ and $H(j4)=1-j$. Compare the response gains applied to $e^{jt}$ and $e^{j4t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: Read the two frequencies separately: $e^{jt}$ uses $H(j1)$, and $e^{j4t}$ uses $H(j4)$. Do not reuse one gain for both inputs.
Now pair each input with its own indexed gain and keep the output frequency unchanged.
The comparison is the gain values themselves: the multiplier is $2$ at frequency $1$ and $1-j$ at frequency $4$. The response changes with frequency.

entries.lesson_title: Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute $H(j\omega)$ as the Fourier transform of the impulse response $h(t)$ and interpret it as the complex gain applied to sinusoidal components at angular frequency $\omega$.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$
sections.section_title: Introduction to Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$

blocks.text: For an LTI system, each angular frequency $\omega$ is handled separately. If a sinusoid at that frequency goes in, the system's effect at that same frequency can be summarized by one complex number, $H(j\omega)$.

That complex number is the frequency response, and it is defined by taking the Fourier transform of the impulse response $h(t)$. In other words, $h(t)$ is the time-domain description of the system, and $H(j\omega)$ is the frequency-by-frequency complex gain extracted from it.

This is the rule to remember for the rest of the topic: compute $H(j\omega)$ by transforming $h(t)$, then read the result as the complex gain applied to each sinusoidal component. Later steps will show how to compute that transform for specific impulse responses and interpret the result as magnitude scaling and phase shift.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$
sections.section_title: Writing $H(j\omega)$ as the Fourier Transform Integral of $h(t)$

example_content.example_prompt: Given $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, write $H(j\omega)$ as the Fourier transform integral that defines the frequency response.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit step $u(t)$: it makes the impulse response causal, so the frequency response is still set up from the Fourier transform definition of $h(t)$. For this step, the goal is only to write the correct integral form, not to evaluate it.
Now substitute the given impulse response and use the fact that $u(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $u(t)=1$ for $t\ge 0$. That changes the support to a one-sided integral over $t\ge 0$.
This is the exact setup the next step will use. The only move here is to recognize the causal support, insert $h(t)$ into the transform kernel, and stop before carrying out the integration.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$
sections.section_title: Computing $H(j\omega)$ from a Simple Impulse Response

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $H(j\omega)$ for $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit step $u(t)$: it tells you the impulse response is causal, so the frequency response comes from the Fourier transform definition of $h(t)$ with one-sided support.
Now combine the decay term and the Fourier kernel into one exponential. That gives a standard one-sided exponential integral with exponent $-(2+j\omega)t$.
So the simple causal exponential has frequency response $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$. This is the compact closed form the next steps can reuse when they compare different impulse responses.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$
sections.section_title: Using a Known Fourier Transform Pair to Find $H(j\omega)$

example_content.example_prompt: Using the known pairs $e^{-t}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $e^{-2t}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, find $H(j\omega)$ for $h(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)+e^{-2t}u(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $h(t)$ is already written as a sum of standard causal exponentials. That means you should use linearity and map each term through a known Fourier transform pair instead of starting a new integral.
Now replace each transform with the matching known pair. Keep the coefficient 2 attached to the first term, and keep the denominator tied to the decay rate in each causal exponential.

So the frequency response is the sum of the two transformed pieces, carried over directly from the known pairs. This is the compact closed form that later questions will vary by changing the coefficients or the standard exponential terms.

sections.lesson_title: Frequency Response as Fourier Transform of $h(t)$
sections.section_title: Interpreting a Computed $H(j\omega)$ as Complex Gain

example_content.example_prompt: If $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, interpret $H(j2)$ as the complex gain applied to the input $e^{j2t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the input $e^{j2t}$, so the input angular frequency is $\omega_0=2$. For a complex exponential, the system effect is read directly from the frequency response at that same frequency: use $H(j\omega_0)$.
To interpret it as a complex gain, put the result in a standard complex form. That makes the multiplier on the sinusoidal component explicit.
So the complex gain on $e^{j2t}$ is $\frac{1-j}{4}$. The output from this sinusoidal component is the same exponential multiplied by that factor.

entries.lesson_title: Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems
entries.lesson_core_move: Use the frequency-response relation $H(j\omega)$ to show that sinusoidal inputs are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, changing only amplitude and phase while keeping frequency unchanged.

sections.lesson_title: Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems
sections.section_title: Introduction to Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems

blocks.text: The cue is a complex exponential input, especially $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$. For an LTI system, the point of this section is to recognize that the system does not change the oscillation into a different frequency; it returns the same oscillation multiplied by a complex scalar.

That is what it means for $x(t)$ to behave like an eigenfunction of the system: the output is only scaled, not reshaped. Here the scalar depends on the input frequency, so the gain is written $H(j\omega)$. You already saw $H(j\omega)$ in the previous lesson, so read it here as the system's complex gain at angular frequency $\omega$.

The important result is that the $e^{j\omega t}$ factor stays intact, so the angular frequency does not change. Only the complex multiplier changes the amplitude and phase, which is the eigenfunction behavior you will reuse when you rewrite sinusoids in complex-exponential form.

sections.lesson_title: Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems
sections.section_title: Checking the Eigenfunction Form for $e^{j\omega t}$

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t}$ and $H(j\omega_0)=3e^{-j\pi/4}$, write the output and state why this is an eigenfunction response.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same-frequency complex exponential $x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t}$. For an LTI system, we use the eigenfunction form from the previous step: the output is the input multiplied by the complex gain at that same frequency, $H(j\omega_0)$.
Here $H(j\omega_0)=3e^{-j\pi/4}$, so substitute that gain and keep the exponential factor unchanged.
The factor $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ is still present, so the angular frequency is unchanged. The complex multiplier changes only the amplitude and phase, which is why this is an eigenfunction response.

sections.lesson_title: Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems
sections.section_title: Applying the Eigenfunction Form to a Cosine Input

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $H(j\omega_0)=2e^{j\pi/6}$, determine the output form and show that the frequency stays $\omega_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real cosine input, $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$. To use the eigenfunction form from the previous step, rewrite the cosine as a pair of complex exponentials so the system response can be applied term by term.
At the positive frequency, the gain is $H(j\omega_0)=2e^{j\pi/6}$. For the matching negative-frequency term, use the conjugate gain $2e^{-j\pi/6}$ so the recombined output stays real.
Now recombine the two exponentials into a cosine. The frequency factor is still $\omega_0$, so only the amplitude and phase have changed.
This is the eigenfunction result in real-signal form: the output is still a cosine at angular frequency $\omega_0$, but the system has scaled it by $2$ and shifted its phase by $\pi/6$.

sections.lesson_title: Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems
sections.section_title: Applying the Eigenfunction Form to a Sine Input

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$ and $H(j\omega_0)=2e^{j\pi/6}$, determine the output form and show that the frequency stays $\omega_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real sine input, $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$. To use the eigenfunction form from the previous step, rewrite the sine as a difference of complex exponentials so the system response can be applied term by term.
At the positive frequency, the gain is $H(j\omega_0)=2e^{j\pi/6}$. For the matching negative-frequency term, use the conjugate gain $2e^{-j\pi/6}$ so the recombined output stays real.
Now recombine the two exponentials into a sine. The frequency factor is still $\omega_0$, so only the amplitude and phase have changed.
This is the eigenfunction result in real-signal form: the output is still a sine at angular frequency $\omega_0$, but the system has scaled it by $2$ and shifted its phase by $\pi/6$.

sections.lesson_title: Sinusoids as Eigenfunctions of LTI Systems
sections.section_title: Recognizing Eigenfunction Behavior from Input and Output Frequency

example_content.example_prompt: Given input $x(t)=\cos(4t)$ and proposed output $y(t)=3\cos(4t-\pi/6)$, decide whether the pair is consistent with eigenfunction behavior and explain the frequency check.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is an input-output pair, so first read the angular frequency from each sinusoid. Here the input is $x(t)=\cos(4t)$ and the proposed output is $y(t)=3\cos(4t-\pi/6)$.
Both signals use the same angular frequency $4$. The output changes only the amplitude, from $1$ to $3$, and the phase, by $-\pi/6$.
That matches eigenfunction behavior for an LTI system: the frequency stays the same, while amplitude and phase are allowed to change. So this pair is consistent with the eigenfunction form.

entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize that a sinusoidal input to a continuous-time LTI system produces an output sinusoid at the same angular frequency, with frequency response affecting only amplitude and phase.

sections.lesson_title: Same-Frequency Output Property
sections.section_title: Introduction to Same-Frequency Output Property

blocks.text: A continuous-time LTI system does not create a new angular frequency from a single sinusoidal input. The output keeps the same coefficient of $t$; only the gain and phase can change.

That is the eigenfunction form: if the input is $x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t}$, then the output is $y(t)=H(j\omega_0)e^{j\omega_0 t}$. The factor $H(j\omega_0)$ can change magnitude and phase, but it does not change $\omega_0$.

So for a real sinusoid, read the input frequency from the coefficient of $t$ and keep that same $\omega_0$ in the output. The amplitude may become $B$, and the phase may shift by $\theta$, but the angular frequency stays fixed for the later examples in this lesson.

sections.lesson_title: Same-Frequency Output Property
sections.section_title: Identifying the Output Angular Frequency from a Single Sinusoidal Input

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system receives $x(t)=2\cos(5t-\pi/3)$. What angular frequency must appear in the output sinusoid?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient of $t$ inside the input sinusoid. For $x(t)=2\cos(5t-\pi/3)$, that coefficient is $5$, so the input angular frequency is $\omega_0=5$.
For a continuous-time LTI system, the amplitude $2$ and the phase $-\pi/3$ can change, but the angular frequency does not. So the output must still use $5$ as the coefficient of $t$.
Therefore, the output angular frequency is $\omega_0=5$.

sections.lesson_title: Same-Frequency Output Property
sections.section_title: Recognizing Same Frequency Despite Amplitude Changes

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system turns $x(t)=\cos(7t)$ into $y(t)=3\cos(7t-\pi/4)$. Which part of the output changed, and which part stayed the same?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient of $t$ in the input cosine. Here $x(t)=\cos(7t)$, so the input angular frequency is $\omega_0=7$.
The factor $3$ changes only the amplitude, and the phase shift $-\pi/4$ changes only the starting angle. The coefficient of $t$ is still $7$, so the output keeps the same angular frequency.
So the part that changed is amplitude, and the part that stayed the same is the angular frequency $7$.

sections.lesson_title: Same-Frequency Output Property
sections.section_title: Recognizing Same Frequency Despite Phase Shifts

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system turns $x(t)=4\sin(3t+\pi/6)$ into $y(t)=4\sin(3t-\pi/3)$. What changed, and what stayed fixed?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient of $t$ in the input sine. Here $x(t)=4\sin(3t+\pi/6)$, so the input angular frequency is $\omega_0=3$.
The phase changes from $\pi/6$ to $-\pi/3$, so the starting angle shifts. The coefficient of $t$ is still $3$, so the output keeps the same angular frequency.
So the phase changed, and the angular frequency stayed fixed at $3$.

sections.lesson_title: Same-Frequency Output Property
sections.section_title: Rejecting Output Sinusoids with New Frequencies

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system receives $x(t)=\cos(2t)$. Which proposed output cannot be correct because it changes the angular frequency?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient of $t$ in the input. Here $x(t)=\cos(2t)$, so the input angular frequency is $\omega_0=2$.

Any proposed output with a different coefficient of $t$ is impossible. For example, a term like $\cos(4t-\pi/3)$ or $\cos(t+\pi/6)$ would change the angular frequency, so it cannot come from this input.
Keep the candidates that preserve $2t$, even if their amplitude or phase changes. A sign flip such as $-\cos(2t)$ still has angular frequency $2$ because it only adds a phase shift.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output sinusoid's amplitude by multiplying the input amplitude by $|H(j\omega)|$ at the input frequency for sinusoidal steady-state passage through an LTI system.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude Scaling by $|H(j\omega)|$
sections.section_title: Introduction to Amplitude Scaling by $|H(j\omega)|$

blocks.text: In sinusoidal steady state through an LTI system, the output sinusoid keeps the same angular frequency $\omega_0$. The change to watch is the amplitude.
For the base case $x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0 t)$, track the input amplitude $A_{\text{in}}$ and the gain magnitude $|H(j\omega_0)|$ at that same frequency.
So the output amplitude is the input amplitude multiplied by the magnitude of the frequency response at $\omega_0$. The output frequency stays fixed at $\omega_0$.
Read the size of $|H(j\omega_0)|$ this way: values less than $1$ mean attenuation, values equal to $1$ mean unity gain, and values greater than $1$ mean amplification.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude Scaling by $|H(j\omega)|$
sections.section_title: Scaling an Amplitude Using a Given $|H(j\omega_0)|$

example_content.example_prompt: A sinusoid with amplitude $A_{\text{in}}=8$ enters an LTI system whose magnitude at the input frequency is $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.5$. Find the output amplitude.

explanation_blocks.text: This is the cleanest numerical case: the gain magnitude is already given, so the only job is to scale the input amplitude.
Read off $A_{\text{in}}=8$ and $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.5$ from the prompt. Then apply the amplitude rule by multiplying those two numbers.
So the output amplitude is $4$.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude Scaling by $|H(j\omega)|$
sections.section_title: Evaluating $|H(j\omega)|$ at the Input Frequency

example_content.example_prompt: A sinusoid $x(t)=5\cos(4t)$ enters an LTI system with $H(j\omega)=\frac{10}{3+j\omega}$. Find the output amplitude.

explanation_blocks.text: This example adds one new wrinkle: the gain factor is not given directly, so first evaluate the frequency response at the input frequency $\omega_0=4$.
Read the input amplitude as $A_{\text{in}}=5$. Then substitute $\omega_0=4$ into $H(j\omega)$ and take the magnitude.
Now apply the amplitude rule with that magnitude: multiply the input amplitude by $2$.
So the output amplitude is $10$.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude Scaling by $|H(j\omega)|$
sections.section_title: Computing $|H(j\omega_0)|$ from a Complex Frequency Response Value

example_content.example_prompt: For an input amplitude $5$, the system response at the input frequency is $H(j\omega_0)=3-4j$. Find the output amplitude.

explanation_blocks.text: This example keeps the same amplitude rule, but the frequency-response value is given in rectangular form. The first job is to extract its magnitude.
Read the input amplitude as $A_{\text{in}}=5$ and recognize that the system response at the same input frequency is $H(j\omega_0)=3-4j$. For a complex number $a+bj$, use $|a+bj|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
Now use that magnitude as the amplitude gain and multiply it by the input amplitude.
So the output amplitude is $25$.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude Scaling by $|H(j\omega)|$
sections.section_title: Identifying Attenuation, Unity Gain, and Amplification from $|H(j\omega_0)|$

example_content.example_prompt: A system has $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.4$ at the input frequency. Decide whether the output amplitude is attenuated, unchanged, or amplified.

explanation_blocks.text: This example keeps the same amplitude rule, but the new job is to classify the gain factor by comparing it with $1$.
Read the gain factor as $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.4$. Since $0.4<1$, the output amplitude is smaller than the input amplitude.
So this system produces attenuation.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output sinusoid's phase by evaluating $\angle H(j\omega)$ at the input frequency and adding that shift to the input phase while leaving the frequency unchanged.

sections.lesson_title: Phase Shifting by $\angle H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Introduction to Phase Shifting by $\angle H(j\omega)$

blocks.text: The previous lesson showed that a complex exponential input keeps the same frequency through an LTI system. Here the new focus is the phase term: the system response $H(j\omega)$ rotates the output at that input frequency.
Write $H(j\omega)$ in polar form so the phase contribution is visible. That lets you see the response as a magnitude factor together with an angle that will be added to the output exponent.
Now multiply the input $e^{j\omega t}$ by that polar form. The angle from $H(j\omega)$ adds directly to the exponent, so the output keeps the same $\omega$ and picks up a phase rotation.
For a real sinusoid, read the same rule as a phase shift on the cosine. Add $\angle H(j\omega)$ to the input phase $\phi$ and keep $\omega$ unchanged.
So the reusable rule is: evaluate $\angle H(j\omega)$ at the input frequency, add it to the input phase, and keep the frequency the same.

sections.lesson_title: Phase Shifting by $\angle H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Adding a Given Phase Shift to an Input Phase

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)=\cos(4t+\pi/6)$ and $\angle H(j4)=\pi/3$, what is the output phase?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system phase shift is already given at the input frequency, so the only move is to add the angles and keep $\omega=4$ unchanged.
So the output phase is $\pi/2$. The output sinusoid still uses the same frequency $4$, so the full cosine form changes only in its phase.

sections.lesson_title: Phase Shifting by $\angle H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Adding a Negative Phase Shift

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)=\cos(2t+\pi/4)$ and $\angle H(j2)=-\pi/6$, what is the output phase?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system phase shift is already given at the input frequency, so a negative value is still added to the input phase. Keep $\omega=2$ unchanged.
So the output phase is $\pi/12$. The negative sign changes the angle, but it does not change the frequency of the sinusoid.

sections.lesson_title: Phase Shifting by $\angle H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Evaluating $\angle H(j\omega)$ at the Input Frequency

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)=\cos(t+\pi/6)$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{1+j\omega}{1-j\omega}$, what is the output phase?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $\angle H(j\omega)$ is not given directly, so first evaluate the transfer function at the input frequency $\omega=1$ and read off its angle. Then add that angle to the input phase.
Now add the evaluated phase shift to the input phase $\pi/6$. The frequency stays at $1$ while only the angle changes.
So the output phase is $2\pi/3$, and the same-frequency output would be $\cos(t+2\pi/3)$.

sections.lesson_title: Phase Shifting by $\angle H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Writing the Same-Frequency Output with the Shifted Phase

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)=A\cos(5t-\pi/3)$ and $\angle H(j5)=\pi/6$, write the output sinusoid.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the phase result from the previous step, then put it back into the cosine. The frequency stays at $5$, so only the phase term changes.
So the output is still the same kind of sinusoid: same amplitude symbol $A$, same angular frequency $5$, and only the phase updated to $-\pi/6$.
